Moment
MOH-ment
n. (an instant of time; rendering Hebrew rega, Greek atomos, parautika)
From Latin momentum, a movement, and by extension the smallest measurable interval — the instant in which a balance tips. The Greek in 1 Corinthians 15:52 is atomos, that which cannot be cut: an indivisible instant.

Biblical Definition

A moment in Scripture is the smallest unit of time, and it is used to measure two things against one another: the brevity of wrath and affliction, and the suddenness of God's decisive acts. On the first, the psalmist sets a divine ratio: “his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). Isaiah counsels the same patience under judgment — “hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast” (Isaiah 26:20). Paul weighs the whole of Christian suffering on that scale and finds it light: “our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17) — written by a man beaten, stoned, shipwrecked, and imprisoned, who is not minimising anything but comparing. The moment is also the unit of God's decisive action, and the resurrection is timed in it: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). The Greek atomos means indivisible — there will be no process, no interval, nothing to observe partway through. The same instant that measures the brevity of grief measures the speed of glory.

Webster 1828 Definition

The smallest unit of time. God's anger endures a moment where His favour is life; Paul weighs all Christian affliction as light and momentary against eternal glory; and the resurrection happens in an atomos, an indivisible instant.

expand to see more

MOMENT, n. [L. momentum, from moveo, to move.] The most minute and indivisible part of time; an instant.

2. Force; impulse; impulsive power.

3. Importance in influence or effect; consequence; weight or value; as a matter of moment.

MOMENTARY, a. Lasting but a moment; done in a moment.

5. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. 1 Cor. 15.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 4:17 — "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;"

1 Corinthians 15:52 — "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed."

Psalm 30:5 — "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."

Isaiah 26:20 — "Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast."

Modern Corruption

2 Corinthians 4:17 is used to hurry the grieving past their grief — your affliction is light and momentary, so stop — which turns Paul's comparison into a dismissal he never made.

expand to see more

The verse is regularly deployed at the wrong moment and with the wrong force, as a rebuke to a Christian whose suffering is not resolving on schedule. Two things are worth noticing about who wrote it. Paul's catalogue in the same letter — stripes above measure, prisons, deaths oft, five times forty stripes save one, thrice beaten with rods, once stoned, thrice shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:23-25) — means light affliction is not the verdict of a comfortable man. And the same letter contains his admission that he was pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that he despaired even of life (2 Corinthians 1:8). The comparison is between two real weights, not a denial that one of them is heavy. Psalm 30:5 shows the right pastoral use: weeping may endure for a night, and the night is granted, named, and not hurried. The believer who is told his grief should already be over has been given the arithmetic without the permission.

There is a second-order misuse in eschatology, where 1 Corinthians 15:52 has been made the anchor text of a secret rapture and a detailed timetable. Paul's in a moment is a statement about the manner of the change, not the schedule of it, and its immediate context is a trumpet, the raising of the dead, and the swallowing up of death in victory — the public and final end. The dictionary holds the bodily second coming, the resurrection of the just and the unjust, and the final judgment, and declines the dispensational scheme that arranges these into stages the New Testament nowhere separates. What the verse gives the believer is better than a timetable: however long the night, the change itself will take no time at all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rega (an instant, a wink), from a root meaning to blink; Greek atomos (indivisible, hence an instant), rhipe (a flick, as of the eye), and parautika (momentary, for the present).

expand to see more

Hebrew rega (H7281) — a moment, instant; the word in Psalm 30:5, Isaiah 26:20, and Isaiah 54:7-8.

Greek atomos (G823) — uncut, indivisible; the noun in 1 Corinthians 15:52 and the source of the English atom.

Greek rhipe (G4493) — a flick, jerk, twinkling; joined to ophthalmos (eye) in the same verse.

Greek parautika (G3910) — for the present, momentary; the adverb in 2 Corinthians 4:17.

Greek baros (G922) — weight, burden; the noun Paul sets against the lightness, an eternal weight of glory.

Usage

"“Light affliction, which is but for a moment” — written by a man five times scourged; a comparison, not a dismissal."

"“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” — atomos, indivisible; there will be nothing to observe partway through."

"“Weeping may endure for a night” — the night is granted, named, and not hurried."
